79.t: Bus to Atlantic City: whisky and twenty-five hamburgers
79.s: On the way to an Atlantic City gig, Waller passed out bottles, stopped a truck for supplies, and had the bus halt at a roadside stand where he ate about 25 hamburgers.
79.q: The Fats Fats Waller. And he's a tremendous personality so we had another gig. We go down to Atlantic City and it's the first time the musicians are on time. Musicians are never on time, you know. Guys I know ain't never on time but sometimes

79.t: Fats Waller's easygoing leadership; "The Fats Waller" at the Apollo
79.s: Thomas describes Waller as definite without forcing his ideas, mentions the later Jitterbug Waltz recording, and recalls the Apollo rehearsal where Fats wanted to be introduced as "the Fats Waller".
79.q: Well, he's a tremendous musician and we had gotten through gigs but the gig that impressed me the most about Fats' personality was the gig at Atlantic City. And, I was worried about his musicianship and all because he was a very (sweet) musician. He's one of the most definite people I've ever…

79.t: Fats Waller's piano sound and the Atlantic City restaurant feast
79.s: Thomas praises Waller's piano sound, then recounts Fats ordering three chickens and three steaks at a restaurant and the waitress setting the table for four, to which Fats replied that no one else was coming.
79.q: I guess it might be but he was a tremendous person. And, somehow there was a little definition between the two of us, something in the trumpet he liked that I was doing and it was easy to like him because he had the greatest sound. And I worked for Tatum and Tatum loved him, you know. But, for…

79.t: Fats Waller's band: Tom Whaley, rehearsals and the left-hand corner
79.s: Thomas worked with Waller only a month or two. He describes early-morning rehearsals under Tom Whaley, Henderson's band as the greatest, and a Yale gig before Waller's Apollo date.
79.q: No. It couldn't have been over a month. I'm almost sure. Maybe allow me two months. May I tell you about this? May I tell you this story? If I may.

79.t: Fats Waller's first big band at the Apollo
79.s: Thomas recalls working with Fats Waller's band out of the Arcadia, its first theater date at the Apollo with Johnny Hamilton, and a confused sequence of Turner, Henderson and Waller.
79.q: Well, we did his first theater date. ... Bugs about Johnny Hamilton. I met him way back in Missouri. He's Fats' favorite trumpet player.

80.t: Fats buying a Christmas outfit for his Pittsburgh barber's family
80.s: Autrey tells how Fats gave his regular barber's wife a coat, the son a coat, and the barber a suit, moving the man to tears.
80.q: Let me think of that, let me think. Well, I've seen -- well I thought -- I think it was in Pittsburgh, one thing -- I think the thing I often think about, we'd get into town, and he would need a shave and a haircut. I don't know for what reason, or who called and told him about this man. He called…

80.t: Fats Waller at Autrey's mother's table and plum tree in Evergreen
80.s: On a Southern tour the Waller band stopped at Evergreen, where his mother and church friends laid on a feast and Fats tried to climb her plum tree.
80.q: Oh man, this would be good. You'll like this. We played, what, Birmingham, Montgomery, Alabama, Birmingham, Alabama, and we were on our way south, going down into Florida, and Mobile, and all that business, and New Orleans, and whatnot. So naturally route one goes right through Evergreen, my home…

80.t: Fats fills the Howard Theater with neighborhood kids and candy
80.s: Fats invited neighborhood kids to the show, bought a hundred pounds of candy, and filled the theater, threatening to walk out on the horrified manager, who then held the show over.
80.q: Quite often. Quite often. I'm trying to think of some more, but I've seen him do a lot of things that were so doggoned nice, and to other people, and -- I thought it was nice. Oh! In Washington, D. C., after we stopped doing sat down one night here, and started doing theaters, well he had three…

81.t: Fats Waller as the closest friend and genius
81.s: Fats Waller stands out; Johnson met him at 19, kept an album inscribed 'To my best friend', and was asked to be head pallbearer.
81.ch: Reel 1: childhood, first songs, Fats Waller
81.q: Oh, he was in his forties when he died; he died very young, you know -- very, very young. But Fats came along at a time -- Fats lived very fast.

81.t: What Fats Waller was like and how publishers loved him
81.s: Fats filled a room, sold the same song to six publishers and no one got angry, and everyone on Broadway loved him.
81.ch: Reel 1: childhood, first songs, Fats Waller
81.q: So he was the most wonderful guy -- I don't know of anyone in my life that publishes on Broadway would do what they did with Fats. Fats would sell the same songs to six publishers, and not one of those publishers would ever get angry with Fats.

81.t: Leaving Chicago for New York; Fats at 19
81.s: Johnson left Chicago at 19 or 20, met Fats Waller at 19 and wrote a song with him the next year.
81.q: Yeah, that I thought I would never meet -- you know, and I didn't know how to go about meeting the person, and lo and behold, you come from Chicago with your chops still wet, you know, and you go to New York, and well -- to tell you the truth, I would say that most of my life has been spent in New…

82.t: Managing Victor's jazz repertoire in 1935; Rollini's tap room gang
82.s: At Victor from 1935 he brought in jazz-minded groups, including Adrian Rollini's tap room gang with Fats Waller at the piano.
82.q: I'll say so. Well, the evolution of jazz in New York, you know, covers a big field. And when I joined Victor, as a manager of autism repertoire in 1935, my job then was to, to sort of lean over backward, to see if the, those people who were jazz minded, couldn't get more product. And it was then…

82.s: He took over Fats Waller in 1938 and recalls six years with him until Fats died on the train from Hollywood in 1943. Kirkeby says they staged the first strictly jazz concert, in Seattle in 1942.
82.q: No, I do not. No, I do not. We had so many bands that day that personnel didn't enter in. It was a matter of getting jobs. We were concerned with. When I took over Fats in 1938, that was the job of the lifetime. Because if ever there was a hunk of talent weighing 285 pounds, who was a genius…

70.t: Fats Waller at the Apollo: Hammond organ, wine bottles and appetite
70.s: The last time Jackson saw Fats was at the Apollo; Waller had a Hammond organ, gave every bandsman a bottle, and ate from serving dishes.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Hammond had just given him an organ. In fact, Hammond built a three manual organ for him in his house, that he had in his house out here. The top manual had a novochord and solo-vox accompaniment on it back there in those days.

70.t: Fats Waller the entertainer, his death and his swing organ
70.s: Waller would have been a TV star; he died on a train in 1943, and played swing organ at the Lafayette Theater and Connie's Inn.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh. Fats was a fantastic, he was one of the most fantastic entertainers. I think if Fats would have lived to the TV era, he would have been a big star on TV. I always have believed this.

83.t: Al Young as Fats Domino's unsung producer and scout
83.s: Matassa credits Al Young with getting Fats Domino recorded, until Lou Chudd dropped him, and notes distributors doubled as talent scouts.
83.q: Well, everybody ignores all of the hard work that he, if you had to credit one person, if you had to credit one person for Fats Domino, it had to be, it has to be Al Young. Mm-hmm.

84.t: Fats Waller at the Lyric Theater and as a pianist
84.s: Fats came to the Lyric Theater and sat in; Handy says he had a good six-piece band and played much real piano behind the clowning, then turns to young players.
84.ch: Offers, Earl Foster and Fats Waller
84.q: Yeah, Fat used to come here to the Lyric Theater. When I was waiting for Beansy. Sure, Fat used to come over there and sit in and play with us a lot of times.

85.t: Fats Waller and the song Nobody Knows
85.s: Carter met Waller in the late twenties, recorded with him with McKinney's, and finished Waller's song with lyricist Bud Allen.
85.q: Gee, I don’t know exactly, but just being around Harlem at the time. Oh, let’s see, it was probably the late twenties, maybe in the mid . . . late twenties, I would say. Then we recorded together for the McKinney’s Cotton Pickers, you know, the thing with Don Redmond, and . . .

86.t: Basie introduces him to the greats; Fats Waller connection
86.s: Basie introduced Edison to Ellington, Armstrong, Fats Waller and others, and told how Waller got him an organ job.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: Armstrong. He introduced me to all the greats. Claude Hopkins, he introduced me to. He introduced me to Buck and Bubbles [a vaudeville partnership between John W. Sublett (stage name John W. Bubbles), known as the “father of rhythm tap” and stride piano player Ford L. “Buck” Washington]. He…

16.s: He thinks he met Waller briefly and recalls him always having a good time.
16.q: I think I did because Strayhorn and I traveled around a lot together, you know, and I think that once at the Hollywood Café or whatever, right across from Dicky, not Dicky Wells… oh, chicken and waffles, what's the name of the place … anyway …

87.t: Jamming with Ellington men and Fats Waller at the hotel
87.s: He recalls Lawrence Brown, Cootie Williams, Johnny Hodges, Arthur Whetsel and Harry Carney, and Fats Waller with a rented organ.
87.ch: Earl Hines, Chicago and later gigs
87.q: Oh, Lawrence and I used to get together, and Cootie, Cootie was younger then. He liked to play a lot, you know, and he'd play a lot. And, of course, Johnny didn't,

88.t: Fats Waller trio at the Famous Door; Fats as godfather
88.s: After Stuff Smith, Lee worked in a Fats Waller trio with bassist Al Morgan, and Fats became godfather to his son.
88.ch: Fats Waller, Nat Cole and Les Hite
88.q: 3 or 4 books while he was here. Then after they left then Fats Waller came out, and Al Morgan was here at the time. Al Morgan used to be bass player with Cab Calloway, so he had quit Cab Calloway here, and we became very good friends, and so he knew Fats from New York, and so Fats was looking for a…

66.t: The Lincoln Theatre with Ellington's Washingtonians, and Fats Waller
66.s: Stranded in New York, she played the Lincoln Theatre in Harlem with Seymour and Jeanette alongside Duke Ellington's Washingtonians and met Fats Waller, who made audiences scream.
66.q: : Yep. We got stranded in New York and so we went back to Pittsburgh, Joe Williams, John, and I, then later on to Memphis with John. During this period is when I met Fats Waller.

89.t: Playing for W.K. Vanderbilt with Fats Waller
89.s: Vanderbilt invited a few musicians and Fats to his house to play, talk about Europe and pay them, and complained that everyone flattered him.
89.q: New York once. I used to play for the rich people in New York in the '30's, you know, and I was playing for the Vanderbilts and I had to go out and play at parties for them. I used to take Fats out with me to Vanderbilt's house all the time.

90.t: Fats Waller and Trombone Smitty at the Paradise
90.s: Fats Waller's local band drank 52 fifths in a week, and Trombone Smitty brought the house down with one eight-bar bridge.
90.q: I also saw Fats Waller at the Paradise Theatre. Heh-heh, I can tell you something real funny about that. He came to Detroit with just his basic group, just the five pieces that he'd use all the time. Sedric... I don't remember the tenor player's name, but his last name was Sedric. [GENE SEDRIC]…

91.t: Fats Waller and becoming a professional
91.s: Fats Waller was active at the Lincoln Theatre; Carter says he was still learning but already professional at 15 or 16.
91.q: Well, it depends upon how you would define genuinely ... certainly it is not synonymous with complete. But you know, I was learning. I was still, of course, undergoing the learning process, which even at this point, I still am -- but that was pretty early.

18.t: Harlem piano school and Cafe Society
18.s: He played with Willie the Lion and three boogie-woogie pianists at Cafe Society.
18.q: Willie the Lion Smith - we worked - I don't know, can't anybody play with Willie the Lion. But we had three piano players, three boogie-woogies, down at Cafe Society.

92.t: Fats Waller's sixteen-piece band jamming at the Three Deuces; Waller at the Howard Theatre
92.s: Waller brought his whole big band, with Al Casey, to jam in the small club, and later Collins saw him led on stage drunk at the Howard Theatre.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Well, he carried a big band, and he played all of the big theatres at this time, you know. And this was during the thirties, you know, and why I mentioned it is because normally, you know, one guy will come in to jam, you know, or maybe two, but Fats brought his whole 16 piece band in to jam. They…

93.t: Walter Beatty and his tap dance walk
93.s: Green describes Walter Beatty, a heavy, light-footed comedian who introduced the tap dance walk with character walks, and partnered Foster.
93.q: He was famous for tap dancing, because he introduced the tap dance walk, see. Otherwise -- if you can walk you can dance, and tap dancing is like walking. So he would demonstrate this, how to walk tap dancing. He's just

94.t: Fats Waller: drinking in Los Angeles and his death
94.s: Moore recalls drinking with Fats at the Lincoln Theater and his prophetic remark before dying on a train.
94.ch: Fats Waller, marriage and Indian school tours
94.q: that we neglected to talk about from the '40s that you knew from the late '30s and '40s -- Fats Waller. We talked between us about him but we didn't really -- tell us some of your friendships with Fats. Oh, Fats, I wish I were he, on the road just like -- the corner of the road. But I ran into Fats…

95.t: Fats Waller, Clarence Williams and Eva Taylor
95.s: She went out often with Fats Waller, Clarence Williams was cautious, and she felt sorry for Eva Taylor under Williams's meanness.
95.ch: Friends, New York life and recording routine
95.q: No. The only thing (unintelligible) he'd come and get me and take me out and I never (unintelligible) about me having a husband. He would get skeptical of talking to me and Clarence Williams (PHONETIC), ________, "Man, don't do this," "Man, don't do that," "Man, don't do --" (Laughter.) "Man,…

96.s: Hungover, Fats asks for gin on stage; McPartland brings it on a tray.
96.ch: Fats Waller, Zululand and the ideal band
96.q: Oh, marvelous man. Just a beautiful man. He played such beautiful organ along with great performing. He could sing and great personality. A great human being. He drank a lot. And as a matter of fact he used to have a little back room there where all us musicians were between sets while somebody…

6.t: First hearing Duke's band; Fats Waller on organ with the pit band
6.s: He first heard Duke's band at the Lincoln Theater, and recalls Fats Waller playing organ together with the pit band, probably at the Lincoln.
6.q: Yeah. Yeah. And that's where I heard -- at the Lincoln Theater -- or was it the Lafayette? Either the Lincoln or the Lafayette, Fats was playing organ, and Fats used to play -- Fats was playing the organ, then the pit band came on. Then they played together, the organ and the pit band, and that was…

75.s: He recalls seeing only the back of Fats Waller at a show and Waller playing sing-alongs on the organ at the Lafayette Theatre.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: See, I go back early, because this is my early childhood... I always go to that...my first realization of it. I remember Fats Waller, the first time I saw him, I saw the back of him -- I saw this fat guy. And I heard it from everybody: 'Have you ever heard Fats Waller?' Well, I'm playing ball then,…

97.s: Scott works three or four weeks with Waller and dislikes the room.
97.q: And I had a pocketful of money and I had put a little money in the bank, and the family was living comfortably and I was happy. All right, here come a call from Chick Webb, opening up at the Savoy. No, no, I'm ahead of myself. Fats Waller, Fats Waller, in between, called me. Come to the Capital.…

76.t: Fats Waller's big band at Connie's Inn
76.s: Zutty returned to Connie's Inn with a big band led by Fats Waller, who played organ and piano, playing all of Fats's tunes.
76.q: Yes. Fats led it because Fats played the organ and the piano. Because he had a big white organ too you know.

98.s: Fats ate steaks at the DeLisa, lived at the Trenier Hotel and served whisky from a pail, according to Leon Washington.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Yeah, right. He would come in the Club DeLisa when we were there, and we had a steam table, and this was when it was on the other side of the street, --
